claim: The effectiveness of artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) to treat Plasmodium falciparum malaria is threatened by resistance.
source: The effectiveness of artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) to treat Plasmodium falciparum malaria is threatened by resistance.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established knowledge in the field.

claim: Drug resistance was more likely to evolve in low transmission settings due to the lower levels of (i) immunity and (ii) within-host competition between genotypes.
source: Drug resistance was more likely to evolve in low transmission settings due to the lower levels of (i) immunity and (ii) within-host competition between genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations and analysis presented in the manuscript, as shown in Figure 4 and discussed in the Results section.

claim: Spread of parasites resistant to artemisinin partner drugs depended on the period of low drug concentration (known as the selection window).
source: Spread of parasites resistant to artemisinin partner drugs depended on the period of low drug concentration (known as the selection window).
evidence: This is supported by model results showing the influence of drug half-life and selection windows on resistance spread.

claim: Spread of partial artemisinin resistance was slowed with prolonged parasite exposure to artemisinin derivatives.
source: Spread of partial artemisinin resistance was slowed with prolonged parasite exposure to artemisinin derivatives and accelerated when the parasite was also resistant to the partner drug.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations showing the effect of drug half-life and treatment duration on resistance spread.

claim: Spread of partial artemisinin resistance was accelerated when the parasite was also resistant to the partner drug.
source: Spread of partial artemisinin resistance was slowed with prolonged parasite exposure to artemisinin derivatives and accelerated when the parasite was also resistant to the partner drug.
evidence: This is demonstrated by model results shown in Figure 2B and discussed in the Results section.

claim: The WHO recommends several artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) to treat uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
source: The WHO recommends several artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) to treat uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria (WHO, 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO guidelines.

claim: ACTs combine a short-acting artemisinin derivative to rapidly reduce parasitaemia during the first 3 days of treatment and a long-acting partner drug to eliminate remaining parasites.
source: ACTs combine a short-acting artemisinin derivative to rapidly reduce parasitaemia during the first 3 days of treatment and a long-acting partner drug to eliminate remaining parasites (WHO, 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO guidelines.

claim: Drug combinations are intended to delay the evolution of drug resistance, which has frequently occurred under monotherapy treatment.
source: These drug combinations are intended to delay the evolution of drug resistance, which has frequently occurred under monotherapy treatment (Farooq and Mahajan, 2004; White, 1999; White, 2004; Wongsrichanalai et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Parasites partially resistant to artemisinin have emerged in the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) and, more recently, in Rwanda, Uganda, Guyana, and Papua New Guinea despite the use of ACTs.
source: However, parasites partially resistant to artemisinin have emerged in the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) and, more recently, in Rwanda, Uganda, Guyana, and Papua New Guinea despite the use of ACTs (WHO, 2020b; Chenet et al., 2016; Uwimana et al., 2020; Uwimana et al., 2021; Miotto et al., 2020; Balikagala et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to WHO reports and published studies.

claim: Partial artemisinin resistance leads to slower parasite clearance following treatment with ACTs, but not necessarily to treatment failure.
source: Partial artemisinin resistance leads to slower parasite clearance following treatment with ACTs, but not necessarily to treatment failure (WHO, 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO guidelines.

claim: High rates of treatment failure have been observed in the GMS due to parasites being less sensitive to artemisinin derivatives and their partner drugs.
source: However, high rates of treatment failure have been observed in the GMS due to parasites being less sensitive to artemisinin derivatives and their partner drugs (WHO, 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO guidelines.

claim: The evolution of drug resistance follows a three-step process of mutation, establishment, and spread.
source: The evolution of drug resistance follows a three-step process of mutation, establishment, and spread.
evidence: This is supported by citations to population genetics literature.

claim: Establishment is a highly stochastic step as the parasite with the drug-resistant mutation needs to infect other hosts.
source: Second, establishment is a highly stochastic step as the parasite with the drug-resistant mutation needs to infect other hosts (zur Wiesch et al., 2011; Mackinnon, 2005; Hastings, 2004; Hastings et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on population genetics.

claim: The resistant strain establishes in the population once its frequency is high enough to minimise its risk of stochastic extinction.
source: The resistant strain establishes in the population once its frequency is high enough to minimise its risk of stochastic extinction (zur Wiesch et al., 2011; Mackinnon, 2005; Hastings, 2004; Hastings et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on population genetics.

claim: In settings with higher heterogeneity of parasite reproductive success, establishment of mutations is less likely because the effects of stochasticity are more substantial.
source: In settings with higher heterogeneity of parasite reproductive success, establishment of mutations is less likely because the effects of stochasticity are more substantial (zur Wiesch et al., 2011; Hastings, 2004; Hastings et al., 2020; Hastings and Mackinnon, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on population genetics.

claim: The more selection favours the resistant strain, the more likely it is to establish.
source: In addition, the more selection favours the resistant strain, the more likely it is to establish (zur Wiesch et al., 2011; Hastings, 2004; Hastings et al., 2020; Hastings and Mackinnon, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on population genetics.

claim: The mutation spreads at a rate that depends on the strength of selection.
source: The mutation spreads at a rate that depends on the strength of selection (zur Wiesch et al., 2011; Hastings et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on population genetics.

claim: Mathematical models of infectious disease have not previously been used to systematically assess the joint influence of multiple factors on the establishment and spread of drug-resistant P. falciparum.
source: Mathematical models of infectious disease have not previously been used to systematically assess the joint influence of multiple factors on the establishment and spread of drug-resistant P. falciparum (e.g. Klein, 2014; Slater et al., 2017; Bushman et al., 2018; Whitlock et al., 2021; Hastings et al., 2002; Watson et al., 2021; Brock et al., 2018; Watkins and Mosobo, 1993; Pongtavornpinyo et al., 2008; White et al., 2009; Chiyaka et al., 2009; Esteva et al., 2009; Koella and Antia, 2003; Lee and Penny, 2019; Lee et al., 2022; Legros and Bonhoeffer, 2016; Tchuenche et al., 2011; Tumwiine et al., 2007) (and to the best of our knowledge other drug-resistant pathogens [virus, bacteria, etc.]).
evidence: This is supported by a review of previous modeling studies cited in the text.

claim: Parasites partially resistant to artemisinin exhibit an extended ring-stage during which they are not sensitive to artemisinin; however, parasites remain sensitive to artemisinin during other stages.
source: Parasites partially resistant to artemisinin exhibit an extended ring-stage during which they are not sensitive to artemisinin; however, parasites remain sensitive to artemisinin during other stages (Klonis et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017; Sá, 2018; Witkowski et al., 2013; Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Parasites resistant to partner drugs have an increased minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), meaning that they are not sensitive to low drug concentrations but remain susceptible to high concentrations of partner drugs.
source: In addition, parasites resistant to partner drugs have an increased minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), meaning that they are not sensitive to low drug concentrations but remain susceptible to high concentrations of partner drugs (Chaorattanakawee et al., 2016; Chaorattanakawee et al., 2015; Tahita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Under monotherapy, access to treatment and degree of resistance of a monotherapy were the main drivers of the spread of resistance.
source: Under monotherapy, access to treatment (the probability of symptomatic cases to receive treatment within 2 weeks from the onset of symptoms) and degree of resistance of a monotherapy were the main drivers of the spread of resistance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the global sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For the short-acting and the long-acting drugs used as monotherapy, the selection coefficient increased with increasing access to treatment.
source: For the short-acting and the long-acting drugs used as monotherapy, the selection coefficient increased with increasing access to treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Higher degrees of resistance of the resistant genotype to the short-acting drug promoted the spread of parasites resistant to the short-acting drug.
source: In addition, higher degrees of resistance of the resistant genotype to the short-acting drug (relative decrease in the resistant genotype Emax compared with the sensitive one) and the long-acting drug (relative increase in the resistant genotype EC50 compared with the sensitive one) promoted the spread of parasites resistant to the short-acting and the long-acting drugs, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Higher degrees of resistance of the resistant genotype to the long-acting drug promoted the spread of parasites resistant to the long-acting drug.
source: In addition, higher degrees of resistance of the resistant genotype to the short-acting drug (relative decrease in the resistant genotype Emax compared with the sensitive one) and the long-acting drug (relative increase in the resistant genotype EC50 compared with the sensitive one) promoted the spread of parasites resistant to the short-acting and the long-acting drugs, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When the short-acting and the long-acting drugs were used in combination, the most important driver of spread was the degree of resistance of both genotypes to the long-acting drug.
source: In this case, the most important driver of spread was the degree of resistance of both genotypes to the long-acting drug (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the global sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The median selection coefficient was below zero when both genotypes were susceptible to the long-acting drug.
source: The median selection coefficient was below zero when both genotypes were susceptible to the long-acting drug (the minimum degree of resistance to the long-acting drug) (Figure 2B), indicating that using an efficient partner drug can limit the spread of artemisinin resistance.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Using an efficient partner drug can limit the spread of artemisinin resistance.
source: The median selection coefficient was below zero when both genotypes were susceptible to the long-acting drug (the minimum degree of resistance to the long-acting drug) (Figure 2B), indicating that using an efficient partner drug can limit the spread of artemisinin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The spread of parasites resistant to the short-acting drug was accelerated when parasites were also resistant to the long-acting drug.
source: The spread of parasites resistant to the short-acting drug was accelerated when parasites were also resistant to the long-acting drug, highlighting that resistance to the long-acting drug can facilitate the spread of artemisinin resistance.
evidence: This is supported by model results shown in Figure 2B and discussed in the text.

claim: Resistance to the long-acting drug can facilitate the spread of artemisinin resistance.
source: The spread of parasites resistant to the short-acting drug was accelerated when parasites were also resistant to the long-acting drug, highlighting that resistance to the long-acting drug can facilitate the spread of artemisinin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results.

claim: Across settings with a low access to treatment, fitness cost had the largest influence on the selection coefficient.
source: Across settings with a low access to treatment, we found that fitness cost had the largest influence on the selection coefficient (Figure 3—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: High fitness costs prevented the spread of resistance.
source: Consequently, high fitness costs prevented the spread of resistance (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: At a high level of access to treatment, the effect of fitness cost was reduced, and drug properties played a critical role in the spread of drug resistance.
source: At a high level of access to treatment, the effect of fitness cost was reduced, and drug properties played a critical role in the spread of drug resistance, and their influence varied for each treatment profile as described below.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3 and related supplementary figures.

claim: For the short-acting drug used as monotherapy, the half-life had an important influence on the rate of spread.
source: For the short-acting drug used as monotherapy, the half-life had an important influence on the rate of spread (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: A long half-life reduced the spread of resistant parasites by extending the period during which the drug killed partially resistant parasites.
source: A long half-life reduced the spread of resistant parasites by extending the period during which the drug killed partially resistant parasites (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The half-life effect was stronger for parasites with a lower degree of resistance.
source: The half-life effect was stronger for parasites with a lower degree of resistance (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), as highly resistant parasites were less affected by the drug.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The spread of the resistant genotype was faster in populations with low adherence to treatment because with fewer treatment doses, the parasite was exposed to the drug for a shorter time, leading to higher parasite survival.
source: Furthermore, the spread of the resistant genotype was faster in populations with low adherence to treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 6) because with fewer treatment doses, the parasite was exposed to the drug for a shorter time, leading to higher parasite survival.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6 and the mechanistic explanation provided.

claim: The time during which the parasite is exposed to artemisinin is a critical driver of the spread of partial artemisinin resistance.
source: Overall, these results highlight that the time during which the parasite is exposed to artemisinin is a critical driver of the spread of partial artemisinin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results on half-life and adherence effects.

claim: For parasites with a low degree of resistance to the long-acting drug used as monotherapy, the drug half-life also had a key influence on the selection coefficient.
source: For parasites with a low degree of resistance to the long-acting drug used as monotherapy, the drug half-life also had a key influence on the selection coefficient (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Long half-lives were associated with large selection coefficients for parasites with a low degree of resistance to the long-acting drug.
source: However, long half-lives were associated with large selection coefficients (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Drugs with a long half-life have an extended period of low drug concentration in treated patients during which only resistant parasites can infect the host.
source: Drugs with a long half-life have an extended period of low drug concentration in treated patients during which only resistant parasites can infect the host.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on pharmacokinetic principles.

claim: The selection window plays a crucial role in the spread of resistance to long-acting drugs.
source: These results confirm that the selection window plays a crucial role in the spread of resistance to long-acting drugs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results on half-life effects for long-acting drugs.

claim: For parasites with a high degree of resistance to the long-acting drug used as monotherapy, the ratio Cmax/EC50 also had an important influence on the rate of spread.
source: For these resistant parasites, the ratio Cmax/EC50 also had an important influence on the rate of spread (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: When the drug had a low Cmax/EC50 ratio, the duration of the drug killing effect was not long enough to ensure the successful clearances of parasites with a higher degree of resistance, favouring their spread.
source: Thus, when the drug had a low Cmax/EC50 ratio, the duration of the drug killing effect was not long enough to ensure the successful clearances of parasites with a higher degree of resistance (higher EC50), favouring their spread (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and the mechanistic explanation provided.

claim: When the genotype was resistant to the short-acting drug in a population that used the short-acting and the long-acting drugs in combination, factors related to the long-acting drug had the most influence on the selection coefficient.
source: When the genotype was resistant to the short-acting drug in a population that used the short-acting and the long-acting drugs in combination, factors related to the long-acting drug had the most influence on the selection coefficient (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: When the Cmax/EC50 ratio of the long-acting drug was large, the duration of the killing effect of the long-acting drug on parasites resistant to the short-acting drug was higher, reducing their spread.
source: When the Cmax/EC50 ratio of the long-acting drug was large, the duration of the killing effect of the long-acting drug on parasites resistant to the short-acting drug was higher, reducing their spread (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The spread of partial resistance to artemisinin strongly depends on the capacity of the partner drug to kill them.
source: These results highlight that the spread of partial resistance to artemisinin strongly depends on the capacity of the partner drug to kill them.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results on combination therapy.

claim: When the parasite was resistant to the short-acting drug, selection coefficients were higher in settings with lower EIR.
source: When the parasite was resistant to the short-acting drug (when used in monotherapy or combination), selection coefficients were higher in settings with lower EIR (Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7.

claim: For parasites with a high degree of resistance to the long-acting drug used in monotherapy, selection coefficients were higher in settings with lower EIR.
source: We observed a similar trend for parasites with a high degree of resistance to the long-acting drug used in monotherapy (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: The proportion of treated infections is higher at lower EIR due to the lower level of immunity.
source: The proportion of treated infections is higher at lower EIR due to the lower level of immunity (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claim: There is a higher proportion of individuals coinfected by both genotypes at higher EIR.
source: Second, there is a higher proportion of individuals coinfected by both genotypes at higher EIR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model structure and transmission dynamics.

claim: Higher level of co-infection enhanced within-host competition between genotypes, which inhibits the multiplication of resistant parasites within hosts due to their fitness cost and thus limits their spread.
source: This higher level of co-infection enhanced within-host competition between genotypes, which inhibits the multiplication of resistant parasites within hosts due to their fitness cost and thus limits their spread.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model results and mechanistic understanding.

claim: The spread of resistant parasites was higher in the seasonal settings than in non-seasonal settings due to the reduction of immunity levels and a decline in within-host competition between genotypes during the low transmission season of the seasonal settings.
source: Similarly, the spread of resistant parasites was higher in the seasonal settings than in non-seasonal settings (Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7) due to the reduction of immunity levels and a decline in within-host competition between genotypes during the low transmission season of the seasonal settings.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7 and the mechanistic explanation provided.

claim: The spread of partial artemisinin resistance is faster in seasonal settings with low transmission levels.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the spread of partial artemisinin resistance is faster in seasonal settings with low transmission levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results on transmission intensity and seasonality effects.

claim: For parasites with a low degree of resistance to the long-acting drug used in monotherapy, selection coefficients were higher in settings with a large EIR.
source: However, for parasites with a low degree of resistance to the long-acting drug used in monotherapy, selection coefficients were higher in settings with a large EIR (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The proportion of patients with low drug concentrations persisting from previous treatments increases at higher EIR where higher infection rates increase the overall usage of treatment.
source: This arises because the proportion of patients with low drug concentrations persisting from previous treatments increases at higher EIR where higher infection rates increase the overall usage of treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8 and the mechanistic explanation provided.

claim: The selection window of the long-acting drug can change the interplay between the transmission setting and the spread of drug resistance.
source: These results highlight that the selection window of the long-acting drug can change the interplay between the transmission setting and the spread of drug resistance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results showing different EIR effects for different degrees of resistance.

claim: The probability of establishment of a mutation depends on two factors: (i) the size of its selection coefficient and (ii) the degree of heterogeneity in the number of parasite offspring.
source: Population genetic theory has shown that the probability of establishment of a mutation depends on two factors: (i) the size of its selection coefficient (i.e. establishment becomes more likely as the mutation becomes more advantageous) and (ii) the degree of heterogeneity in the number of parasite offspring.
evidence: This is supported by citations to population genetics theory.

claim: Higher heterogeneity increases stochastic fluctuations of allele number, so increases the chance that the mutation is lost despite its advantage.
source: This occurs because higher heterogeneity increases stochastic fluctuations of allele number, so increases the chance that the mutation is lost despite its advantage (zur Wiesch et al., 2011; Hastings, 2004; Hastings et al., 2020; Hastings and Mackinnon, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to population genetics theory.

claim: The establishment of a mutation was more probable when its selection coefficient was high.
source: As expected, the establishment of a mutation was more probable when its selection coefficient was high (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 4.

claim: For each treatment profile, the probability of establishment of mutations with similar selection coefficients was higher at low EIR than at high EIR.
source: For each treatment profile, the probability of establishment of mutations with similar selection coefficients was higher at low EIR than at high EIR (Figure 4), especially for mutations with a high selection coefficient.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The lower probability of establishment in higher transmission settings suggests that higher transmission levels increase the heterogeneity in parasite reproductive success, reducing the chance to transmit advantageous mutations.
source: The lower probability of establishment in higher transmission settings suggests that higher transmission levels increase the heterogeneity in parasite reproductive success, reducing the chance to transmit advantageous mutations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results shown in Figure 4.

claim: In higher transmission settings, there is higher variability in the number of parasites with distinct genotypes carried by a host and which are competing for reproductive success.
source: First, in higher transmission settings, there is higher variability in the number of parasites with distinct genotypes carried by a host and which are competing for reproductive success.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model structure and transmission dynamics.

claim: Settings with a high EIR have a large variation in the level of individual immunity.
source: Second, settings with a high EIR have a large variation in the level of individual immunity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model structure and immunity dynamics.

claim: Host immunity influences parasite reproductive success by reducing parasite growth within the human host.
source: Host immunity influences parasite reproductive success by reducing parasite growth within the human host.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of malaria immunity.

claim: Evolution of resistance to ACTs begins with the establishment and spread of parasites resistant to the partner drug and once the protective effect of the partner drug is reduced, drug selection falls on the artemisinin component, and parasites then start to acquire resistance to artemisinin derivatives.
source: Our results support the belief that evolution of resistance to ACTs begins with the establishment and spread of parasites resistant to the partner drug and once the protective effect of the partner drug is reduced, drug selection falls on the artemisinin component, and parasites then start to acquire resistance to artemisinin derivatives (e.g. Watson et al., 2021; Hastings et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by model results and citations to previous studies.

claim: Resistance to the partner drug depends on the period of low concentration of this drug during which only resistant parasites can multiply within the host (known as the selection window).
source: First, resistance to the partner drug depends on the period of low concentration of this drug during which only resistant parasites can multiply within the host (known as the selection window).
evidence: This is supported by model results on the effects of drug half-life.

claim: Artemisinin derivatives are short-acting, so they cannot prevent patients from being reinfected by parasites resistant to the partner drug during the selection window.
source: As artemisinin derivatives are short-acting, they cannot prevent patients from being reinfected by parasites resistant to the partner drug during this selection window.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pharmacokinetic properties of artemisinin derivatives.

claim: Resistance to the partner drug was the most critical factor that enhanced establishment and spread of partial artemisinin resistance.
source: Second, resistance to the partner drug was the most critical factor that enhanced establishment and spread of partial artemisinin resistance.
evidence: This is supported by model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Without resistance to the partner drug, parasites partially resistant to artemisinin could only spread at a low rate as the partner drug could still eliminate them, thereby removing their selective advantage.
source: Without resistance to the partner drug, parasites partially resistant to artemisinin could only spread at a low rate as the partner drug could still eliminate them, thereby removing their selective advantage.
evidence: This is supported by model results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Parasites resistant to partner drugs (piperaquine and mefloquine) were already present in the GMS before partial artemisinin resistance emerged.
source: Our results are in line with recent molecular data which show that parasites resistant to partner drugs (piperaquine and mefloquine) were already present in the GMS before partial artemisinin resistance emerged and that the spread of resistance to artemisinin accelerated when it became linked to resistance to the partner drugs (Amato et al., 2018; Hamilton et al., 2019; Wongsrichanalai and Meshnick, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular studies.

claim: The spread of resistance to artemisinin accelerated when it became linked to resistance to the partner drugs in the GMS.
source: Our results are in line with recent molecular data which show that parasites resistant to partner drugs (piperaquine and mefloquine) were already present in the GMS before partial artemisinin resistance emerged and that the spread of resistance to artemisinin accelerated when it became linked to resistance to the partner drugs (Amato et al., 2018; Hamilton et al., 2019; Wongsrichanalai and Meshnick, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular studies.

claim: The presence of partner drug resistance has probably facilitated the spread of resistance to artemisinin in the GMS.
source: Thus, the presence of partner drug resistance has probably facilitated the spread of resistance to artemisinin in the GMS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results and molecular data.

claim: In Africa, to date, only a low degree of resistance to the most commonly used partner drugs (lumefantrine and amodiaquine) are present.
source: In contrast, in Africa, to date, only a low degree of resistance to the most commonly used partner drugs (lumefantrine and amodiaquine) are present (WHO, 2020b; Ehrlich et al., 2021), which has likely limited establishment of resistance to artemisinin derivatives.
evidence: This is supported by citations to WHO reports and published studies.

claim: Low degree of resistance to partner drugs in Africa has likely limited establishment of resistance to artemisinin derivatives.
source: In contrast, in Africa, to date, only a low degree of resistance to the most commonly used partner drugs (lumefantrine and amodiaquine) are present (WHO, 2020b; Ehrlich et al., 2021), which has likely limited establishment of resistance to artemisinin derivatives.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results and epidemiological data.

claim: The evolution of drug resistance in the GMS may have been favoured by the low transmission intensity.
source: We additionally note that the evolution of drug resistance in the GMS may have been favoured by the low transmission intensity (annual EIR range approximate from less than 1 to 25 inoculations per person per year [Edwards et al., 2019a; Chaumeau et al., 2018; Edwards et al., 2019b]) compare to Africa where the transmission intensity is overall higher (annual EIR range from less than 1 to more than 500 inoculations per person per year [Hay et al., 2000; Yamba et al., 2020]).
evidence: This is supported by model results and citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Establishment of drug resistance was more likely in low transmission settings due to the reduced level of within-host competition between genotypes, as well as population immunity.
source: Similar to previous studies (White, 1999; Bushman et al., 2018; Pongtavornpinyo et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2022; Hastings, 1997), establishment of drug resistance in our model was more likely in low transmission settings due to the reduced level of within-host competition between genotypes, as well as population immunity.
evidence: This is supported by model results and citations to previous studies.

claim: A key strategy to mitigate the evolution of partial artemisinin resistance is to ensure that the partner drug efficiently kills the partially resistant parasite.
source: Our results suggest that a key strategy to mitigate the evolution of partial artemisinin resistance is to ensure that the partner drug efficiently kills the partially resistant parasite.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results.

claim: To delay the establishment of artemisinin resistance in Africa and to mitigate the spread of partial artemisinin resistance in regions where it is already established, we should ensure that limited or no genotypes are resistant to the partner drug for first-line ACT.
source: Therefore, to delay the establishment of artemisinin resistance in Africa and to mitigate the spread of partial artemisinin resistance in regions where it is already established, we should ensure that limited or no genotypes are resistant to the partner drug for first-line ACT.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results.

claim: Robust molecular surveillance of resistance markers should be implemented to ensure limited resistance to partner drugs.
source: One approach to ensure this is to implement robust molecular surveillance of resistance markers and to specify more sustainable treatment policies, such as changing first-line ACTs upon detection of resistance or when the frequency of resistant parasites reach a threshold as recommended by the WHO (WHO, 2020b).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results and WHO guidelines.

claim: Adherence should continue to be promoted, as lower treatment compliance can lead to treatment failure even in the absence of resistance to the partner drug.
source: Furthermore, consistent with our results, adherence should continue to be promoted, as lower treatment compliance can lead to treatment failure even in the absence of resistance to the partner drug (WHO, 2020b; Siddiqui et al., 2015; Bruxvoort et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by model results and citations to previous studies.

claim: Future antimalarial therapies should shorten the selection windows of long-acting partner drugs.
source: Our results suggest that future antimalarial therapies should shorten the selection windows of long-acting partner drugs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results.

claim: Resistance to long-acting drugs is the first step in the evolution of resistance to ACTs, and it depends mainly on the length of the selection window.
source: We show that resistance to long-acting drugs is the first step in the evolution of resistance to ACTs, and it depends mainly on the length of the selection window.
evidence: This is supported by model results.

claim: The selection window strongly depends on the drug half-life.
source: We confirm that the selection window strongly depends on the drug half-life, also consistent with previous studies (White, 1999; Slater et al., 2017; Hastings et al., 2002; Watkins and Mosobo, 1993; Pongtavornpinyo et al., 2008; Kay and Hastings, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by model results and citations to previous studies.

claim: Reducing the half-life of the partner drug in an ACT regimen could reduce the spread of resistance.
source: Consequently, reducing the half-life of the partner drug in an ACT regimen could reduce the spread of resistance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results on selection windows.

claim: Unless selection windows are substantially minimised or completely eliminated, the evolution of resistance would not totally be prevented.
source: However, unless selection windows are substantially minimised or completely eliminated, the evolution of resistance would not totally be prevented (Kay and Hastings, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A more sustainable option for ACTs would be to use TACTs (triple artemisinin-based combination therapies).
source: Thus, a more sustainable option for ACTs would be to use TACTs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results and discussion.

claim: TACTs involve combining an artemisinin derivative with two long-acting drugs.
source: TACTs involve combining an artemisinin derivative with two long-acting drugs (Krishna, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The two long-acting drugs in TACTs should have matching half-lives to ensure that parasites are not exposed to residual drug concentrations of only one of the two partner drugs.
source: If or when TACTs are to be widely used, our results emphasise that the two long-acting drugs should have matching half-lives to ensure that parasites are not exposed to residual drug concentrations of only one of the two partner drugs (noting that this is simple in principle, but more difficult in practice [Hastings and Hodel, 2014]).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The parasite population should be devoid of parasites resistant to either of the two long-acting drugs when TACTs are used.
source: In addition, the parasite population should be devoid of parasites resistant to either of the two long-acting drugs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results and discussion.

claim: If resistance to one partner drug already exists in the population, the second partner drug would not be protected, and mutations conferring resistance to this second drug could be selected.
source: If resistance to one partner drug already exists in the population, the second partner drug would not be protected, and mutations conferring resistance to this second drug could be selected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model results and discussion.

claim: Another approach to delay the evolution of partial artemisinin resistance could focus on extending the period of action of artemisinin derivatives.
source: Another approach to delay the evolution of partial artemisinin resistance could focus on extending the period of action of artemisinin derivatives.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results.

claim: The spread of partially resistant genotypes decreased when the drug was present in patients for a longer time, such as if it had a long half-life and there was proper treatment adherence.
source: In our monotherapy analysis on the spread of a genotype partially resistant to artemisinin, we found that the spread of partially resistant genotypes decreased when the drug was present in patients for a longer time, such as if it had a long half-life and there was proper treatment adherence.
evidence: This is supported by model results on the effects of half-life and adherence.

claim: Partially resistant parasites are still affected by artemisinin derivatives.
source: This result arises because partially resistant parasites are still affected by the drug (Klonis et al., 2013; Sá, 2018; Witkowski et al., 2013; Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Increasing exposure to artemisinin derivatives leads to higher killing of partially resistant parasites and reduced spread.
source: Thus, increasing their exposure to the drug leads to higher killing and reduced spread.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model results and mechanism of partial resistance.

claim: Increasing the exposure to artemisinin derivatives can be achieved by using the artemisinin derivative having the longest half-life and by increasing the number of doses and days that patients receive treatment.
source: Increasing the exposure to artemisinin derivatives can be achieved by using the artemisinin derivative having the longest half-life and, as highlighted in other studies (Kay et al., 2015; Dogovski et al., 2015; Khoury et al., 2020), can be done by increasing the number of doses and days that patients receive treatment.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results and citations to previous studies.

claim: Extending the dosage regimen will be efficient only with adequate adherence to treatment, which may be challenging to achieve in practice.
source: However, it is worth noting that extending the dosage regimen will be efficient only with adequate adherence to treatment, which may be challenging to achieve in practice.
evidence: This is a caveat based on practical considerations.

claim: For selection coefficients lower than 0.2, the probability of establishment is approximately equal to twice the selection coefficient under the assumption that the number of secondary infections follows a Poisson distribution.
source: Under this assumption, for selection coefficients lower than 0.2 (according to an informal literature review in Hastings et al., 2020, most selection coefficient estimates for malaria drug resistance mutations from the field fall between 0.02 and 0.12), the probability of establishment is approximately equal to twice the selection coefficient (Hastings, 2004; Crow and Motoo, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to population genetics theory.

claim: For selection coefficients lower than 0.2, the probability of establishment was equal to 0.87 times the selection coefficient in this study.
source: In this modelling study, we were uniquely able to quantify the link between selection coefficients and the probability of establishment of mutations. On average, we estimated that, for selection coefficients lower than 0.2, the probability of establishment was equal to 0.87 times the selection coefficient.
evidence: This is supported by model results on the probability of establishment.

claim: The variation in the number of secondary infections of P. falciparum must be much greater than the Poisson distribution assumed by standard population genetics models, and this higher variation reduces the probability of establishment of emerging mutations.
source: Therefore, our findings suggest that the variation in the number of secondary infections of P. falciparum must be much greater than the Poisson distribution assumed by standard population genetics models, and this higher variation reduces the probability of establishment of emerging mutations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of model results with population genetics theory.

claim: Higher heterogeneity in parasite reproductive success may exist in the real-world than as simulated in the model due to factors not captured by the model (such as geographical heterogeneity of exposure to mosquito bites).
source: Note that higher heterogeneity in parasite reproductive success may exist in the real-world than as simulated in our model due to factors not captured by our model (such as geographical heterogeneity of exposure to mosquito bites).
evidence: This is a speculation about model limitations.

claim: Additional factors not captured by the model may further decrease the probability of establishment.
source: These factors may further decrease the probability of establishment (Klein, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The drug action model does not capture stage-specific killing effects.
source: First, our drug action model does not capture stage-specific killing effects, so we could not model parasites partially resistant to artemisinin being insensitive to the drug only during extended ring-stage (Klonis et al., 2013; Sá, 2018; Witkowski et al., 2013; Ye et al., 2016), although previous analyses suggested this would be captured by our variation in the maximum killing rate (Hodel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a limitation of the model acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The model did not capture the impact of artemisinin resistance on gametocytes.
source: Second, our model did not capture the impact of artemisinin resistance on gametocytes.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Patients infected with parasites partially resistant to artemisinin exhibit higher gametocyte densities than patients infected with sensitive parasites.
source: Previous studies have highlighted that artemisinin kills gametocytes, and patients infected with parasites partially resistant to artemisinin exhibit higher gametocyte densities than patients infected with sensitive parasites (Ashley et al., 2014; Witmer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The impact of artemisinin resistance on gametocytes is likely to accelerate the spread of partial resistance.
source: This effect is likely to accelerate the spread of partial resistance.
evidence: This is a speculation about the impact of a model limitation.

claim: OpenMalaria does not capture the recombination of P. falciparum parasites in mosquitoes.
source: Third, our model, OpenMalaria, does not capture the recombination of P. falciparum parasites in mosquitoes (it does not track different genotypes in mosquitoes, and the genotype of a new infections is based on the genotype frequency in humans).
evidence: This is a limitation of the model acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The model can only investigate the spread of resistance at one locus at a time because of the lack of recombination modeling.
source: In practice, this means we can only investigate the spread of resistance at one locus at a time (because if there is no genetic variability at other loci, then the lack of recombination has no impact).
evidence: This is an explanation of a model limitation.

claim: When multiple mutations are needed to confer drug resistance, recombination can slow the spread of drug resistance by separating these mutations.
source: When multiple mutations are needed to confer drug resistance, recombination can slow the spread of drug resistance by separating these mutations (Hastings, 1997; Dye and Williams, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Resistance to some partner drugs requires multiple mutations.
source: Resistance to some partner drugs requires multiple mutations (WHO, 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO guidelines.

claim: Recombination is more likely to impact the spread of resistant parasites in high transmission settings where recombination between different parasite genotypes is more likely.
source: Recombination is more likely to impact the spread of resistant parasites in high transmission settings where recombination between different parasite genotypes is more likely.
evidence: This is an inference based on transmission dynamics.

claim: In high transmission settings, the model probably overestimated the probability of establishment of resistant parasites that have multiple mutations involved in the drug-resistant phenotype.
source: A consequence of not including recombination is that in high transmission settings, we have probably overestimated the probability of establishment of resistant parasites that have multiple mutations involved in the drug-resistant phenotype.
evidence: This is a speculation about the impact of a model limitation.

claim: The difference between the probabilities of establishment in low and high transmission settings is likely greater than reported in this study.
source: This means that the difference between the probabilities of establishment in low and high transmission settings is likely greater than reported here.
evidence: This is a speculation about the impact of a model limitation.

claim: The model may have overestimated the spread of resistant parasites with multiple mutations when these mutations are present in low frequencies.
source: In addition, we may have overestimated the spread of these resistant parasites when these mutations are present in low frequencies.
evidence: This is a speculation about the impact of a model limitation.

claim: The model investigated the establishment of drug-resistant parasites through importation.
source: Lastly, to investigate the establishment of drug-resistant parasites, we modelled the emergence of mutations through importation.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: The estimations represent the establishment of mutations imported into a population or mutations emerging in mosquitoes.
source: Consequently, our estimations represent the establishment of mutations imported into a population or mutations emerging in mosquitoes (assuming that the mosquito has only transmitted the mutated genotype and not the wild type genotype to the individual).
evidence: This is an explanation of what the model results represent.

claim: A mutation emerging during the blood-stage within the human host may have a lower probability of establishment because sensitive parasites would be present in the host, leading to competition between them.
source: A mutation emerging during the blood-stage within the human host may have a lower probability of establishment because sensitive parasites would be present in the host, leading to competition between them.
evidence: This is a speculation about a scenario not modeled.

claim: The probabilities of establishment estimated in this study are consistent with the probabilities of establishment estimated by a previous study.
source: Nevertheless, the probabilities of establishment estimated in this study are consistent with the probabilities of establishment estimated by a previous study (Hastings, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a comparison with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutations conferring malaria drug resistance are more likely to establish in low transmission settings.
source: In summary, our results confirm that mutations conferring malaria drug resistance are more likely to establish in low transmission settings.
evidence: This is a summary of model results.

claim: The establishment and spread of resistance to artemisinin derivatives have likely been facilitated by pre-existing resistance to partner drugs.
source: Our results demonstrate that the establishment and spread of resistance to artemisinin derivatives have likely been facilitated by pre-existing resistance to partner drugs.
evidence: This is a summary of model results.

claim: It is essential to prioritise monitoring and to limit the spread of resistance to partner drugs in current or future ACT regimens.
source: Thus, it is essential to prioritise monitoring and to limit the spread of resistance to partner drugs in current or future ACT regimens.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results.

claim: If resistance to the partner drug is confirmed, response strategies should prioritise monitoring molecular markers and treatment failure and switching to an ACT with an effective partner drug should be considered.
source: If resistance to the partner drug is confirmed, response strategies should prioritise monitoring molecular markers and treatment failure and switching to an ACT with an effective partner drug should be considered.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results.

claim: Drug properties play an essential role in the evolution of drug resistance.
source: In addition, our results show that drug properties play an essential role in the evolution of drug resistance.
evidence: This is a summary of model results.

claim: The ongoing development of new antimalarial combinations should limit selection windows of partner drugs by matching half-lives.
source: Thus, the ongoing development of new antimalarial combinations should limit selection windows of partner drugs by matching half-lives, hopefully leading to longer lasting combination treatments against malaria.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results.

claim: For existing ACTs, it would be advantageous to increase the time of parasite exposure to the short-acting artemisinin derivate and/or to include a second long-acting partner drug with a matching half-life to the other long-acting partner drug.
source: In the medium-term, for existing ACTs, it would be advantageous to increase the time of parasite exposure to the short-acting artemisinin derivate and/or to include a second long-acting partner drug with a matching half-life to the other long-acting partner drug (triple ACTs Krishna, 2019) and for which limited or no parasite resistance exists in the target population.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the model results.
